intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant Parkinson disease-8 (PARK8) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the LRRK2 gene on chromosome 12q12.

paragraphs.text: PARK8 is an autosomal dominant form of Parkinson disease with incomplete penetrance. It usually presents as typical levodopa-responsive parkinsonism with bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and impaired postural reflexes, and a clinical picture that closely resembles idiopathic Parkinson disease (Wszolek et al., 1995; Funayama et al., 2002). The neuropathology varies widely, even within a single family. Reported findings include Lewy body Parkinson disease, diffuse Lewy body disease, nigral degeneration without distinctive histopathology, and pathology resembling progressive supranuclear palsy (Zimprich et al., 2004).

paragraphs.text: Funayama et al. (2002) assigned the name PARK8 to the locus they mapped on chromosome 12 in a Japanese family with autosomal dominant parkinsonism. Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2004) named the protein encoded by the PARK8 gene dardarin, from the Basque word 'dardara', meaning tremor. They chose the name because of the tremor seen in Parkinson disease and because several of their families were of Basque descent. Zimprich et al. (2004) called the gene LRRK2 (leucine-rich repeat kinase-2).

paragraphs.text: Wszolek et al. (1995) studied a family (family D) whose ancestors probably came to the United States from England. The pedigree contained 188 individuals over 6 generations, 18 of whom were affected. Affected members developed typical levodopa-responsive Parkinson disease with bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and impaired postural reflexes. Eye movement abnormalities, pyramidal and cerebellar signs, sensory disturbances, and orthostatic blood pressure changes did not occur. The disease progressed slowly. PET with (18F)-6-fluoro-L-dopa in 1 affected individual showed decreased fluorodopa uptake in a pattern consistent with Parkinson disease. Autopsy of another affected individual showed neuronal and pigmentary loss, gliosis, and Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra pars compacta.

The clinical features did not differ from those of common Parkinson disease, but the neuropathology did. In autopsied cases, loss of melanin-containing cells was mild to moderate, neurons of the locus ceruleus were preserved, and no Lewy bodies were found in any region where they are commonly seen in Parkinson disease.

paragraphs.text: Alcalay et al. (2009) studied 925 patients with early-onset Parkinson disease (onset before age 51 years) from 13 movement disorder centers. Of these, 34 (3.7%) carried the G2019S mutation, 1 of them homozygous. Compared with noncarriers, carriers had a lower tremor score (P = 0.03) and were more likely to have the postural instability and gait difficulty (PIGD) motor phenotype (92.3% vs 58.9%; P = 0.003). The association remained after adjustment for disease duration and Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry (odds ratio, 17.7; P less than 0.001). Carriers and noncarriers had similar age at onset, disease duration, motor scores on the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS), and Mini-Mental State Examination scores.

paragraphs.text: Marras et al. (2011) used a family study design to examine G2019S probands and their first-degree relatives. Tremor was more often a presenting feature in 25 individuals with LRRK2-associated Parkinson disease than in 84 with idiopathic Parkinson disease. Compared with the idiopathic patients, the LRRK2 patients had better olfactory identification, higher Beck Depression Inventory scores, and higher error scores on the Farnsworth-Munsell 100-Hue test of color discrimination. Postural or action tremor was more common in 29 nonmanifesting carriers than in 53 noncarrier family members. The tremor finding contrasts with the lower tremor scores in G2019S carriers reported by Alcalay et al. (2009).

They found neither this mutation nor other known LRRK2 mutations in Japanese patients with sporadic Parkinson disease.

checks.claim: Funayama et al. (2005) found a missense mutation in the kinase domain of LRRK2 in members of the Sagamihara family with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease.
checks.evidence_quote: We detected a missense mutation in the kinase domain of the LRRK2 gene in members with autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease of the Japanese family (the Sagamihara family)
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: The Sagamihara family is a Japanese family that was originally used to define the PARK8 locus.
checks.evidence_quote: We performed genomewide linkage analysis of a Japanese family with autosomal dominant parkinsonism
checks.explanation: The abstract confirms a Japanese family was used to define PARK8 but never calls it the 'Sagamihara' family; only the abstract was supplied.

checks.evidence_quote: We did not detect this mutation or other known mutations of the LRRK2 gene in Japanese patients with sporadic Parkinson's disease.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

paragraphs.text: Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2005) sequenced all 51 coding exons of LRRK2 in 23 probands from families with dominantly inherited Parkinson disease. Three probands carried heterozygous mutations: 2 had G2019S and 1 had a novel I1371V substitution. In a large family, G2019S segregated completely with Parkinson disease. The disease in all 3 families had a phenotype indistinguishable from typical Parkinson disease but a very variable age at onset, which APOE genotype did not explain. Four common coding LRRK2 polymorphisms showed no association with Parkinson disease in 121 patients and 250 controls.

checks.claim: Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2005) sequenced all 51 coding exons of LRRK2 in 23 probands from families with dominantly inherited Parkinson disease.
checks.evidence_quote: All 51 LRRK2 coding exons were sequenced in 23 probands and the mutation frequencies were evaluated in 180 neurologically normal control subjects.
checks.explanation: The objective says the probands came from families showing dominant inheritance of PD.

checks.claim: Three of 23 probands with dominantly inherited Parkinson disease carried heterozygous LRRK2 mutations.
checks.evidence_quote: The authors identified three probands with heterozygous LRRK2 mutations: two of them have the known G2019S substitution and one proband has a novel I1371V substitution.
checks.explanation: Three of the 23 sequenced probands carried heterozygous mutations.

checks.claim: Two probands with dominantly inherited Parkinson disease carried the heterozygous LRRK2 G2019S mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: The authors identified three probands with heterozygous LRRK2 mutations: two of them have the known G2019S substitution
checks.explanation: Two probands carried heterozygous G2019S.

checks.claim: One proband with dominantly inherited Parkinson disease carried a novel heterozygous LRRK2 I1371V substitution.
checks.evidence_quote: three probands with heterozygous LRRK2 mutations: two of them have the known G2019S substitution and one proband has a novel I1371V substitution.
checks.explanation: One proband carried the novel heterozygous I1371V substitution.

checks.claim: LRRK2 G2019S segregated completely with Parkinson disease in a large family.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutation analysis of a large family demonstrated complete segregation of the G2019S with PD.
checks.explanation: The paper states complete segregation of G2019S with PD in a large family.

checks.claim: In the 3 families with LRRK2 mutations (G2019S or I1371V), the disease phenotype was indistinguishable from typical Parkinson disease.
checks.evidence_quote: The disease in the families reported here presents a phenotype indistinguishable from typical PD.
checks.explanation: The phenotype in the reported families matched typical PD.

checks.claim: In the 3 families with LRRK2 mutations (G2019S or I1371V), age at onset was very variable.
checks.evidence_quote: All three families demonstrate a very variable age at onset that is not explained by APOE genotypes.
checks.explanation: All three families showed a very variable age at onset.

checks.claim: APOE genotype did not explain the variable age at onset in the families with LRRK2 mutations.
checks.evidence_quote: All three families demonstrate a very variable age at onset that is not explained by APOE genotypes.
checks.explanation: APOE genotypes did not explain the variable age at onset.

checks.claim: Four common coding LRRK2 polymorphisms showed no association with Parkinson disease in 121 patients and 250 controls.
checks.evidence_quote: the authors genotyped four coding LRRK2 polymorphisms in 250 normal control subjects and 121 patients with PD
checks.explanation: The results add that none of the 4 polymorphisms was associated with PD (p > 0.17).

paragraphs.text: Farrer et al. (2005) genotyped 786 Parkinson disease probands, 32 affected sibs, 1,044 unaffected sibs, and 278 unrelated controls for 9 LRRK2 mutations. They found mutations in 6 probands, 1 affected sib, 1 unaffected sib, and 1 unrelated control, and concluded that LRRK2 mutations only rarely cause idiopathic Parkinson disease.

checks.evidence_quote: the authors studied 786 PD probands, 32 affected siblings, 1,044 unaffected siblings, and 278 unrelated controls. The authors designed allelic discrimination assays for nine LRRK2 mutations

checks.evidence_quote: Thus LRRK2 mutations only rarely cause idiopathic PD.
checks.explanation: The draft restates the authors' conclusion.

paragraphs.text: Lesage et al. (2009) sequenced all 51 coding exons of LRRK2 in index cases from 226 families with Parkinson disease compatible with autosomal dominant inheritance, mostly from France (182) and North Africa (14). They identified 79 sequence variants, 29 of them novel. Eight potentially or proven pathogenic mutations were found in 22 probands (9.7%). G2019S was present in 13 probands (5.8%), 6 of them from North Africa (43%). The known heterozygous R1441H and I1371V mutations were each found in 2 probands, and E334K in 1 patient. Four novel substitutions were considered potentially pathogenic (S52F, N363S, I810V, R1325Q), whereas 2 others (H1216R, T1410M) were probably not causative.

checks.evidence_quote: We performed extensive mutation analyses of all 51 coding exons of the LRRK2 gene in index cases from 226 Parkinson's disease families compatible with autosomal dominant inheritance

checks.evidence_quote: Eight potentially or proven pathogenic mutations were found in 22 probands (9.7%).
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: LRRK2 G2019S was present in 13 probands (5.8%) in the Lesage et al. (2009) study.
checks.evidence_quote: The common p.G2019S mutation was identified in 13 probands (5.8%) including six from North Africa (43%).
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

paragraphs.text: Ishihara et al. (2006) described Parkinson disease patients homozygous for the LRRK2 G2019S mutation: 23 Tunisians, 2 Algerians, 2 US patients, 1 Canadian, and 1 Moroccan. They saw no differences between the homozygous and previously described heterozygous phenotypes, and concluded that the findings did not support a gene dosage effect.

checks.claim: Ishihara et al. (2006) described Parkinson disease patients homozygous for LRRK2 G2019S: 23 Tunisians, 2 Algerians, 2 US patients, 1 Canadian, and 1 Moroccan.
checks.evidence_quote: Patients with familial PD and homozygous LRRK2 mutations included 23 Tunisians, 2 Algerians, 2 US patients, 1 Canadian, and 1 Moroccan.
checks.explanation: The abstract gives these exact counts by country. The objectives state that the patients carry homozygous G2019S.

checks.claim: Ishihara et al. (2006) saw no differences between the phenotypes of LRRK2 G2019S homozygotes and previously described heterozygotes.
checks.evidence_quote: There were no observable differences between the homozygote and heterozygote phenotypes.
checks.explanation: The objectives say the homozygotes were compared with previously published descriptions of heterozygous patients, and the results report no observable differences.

checks.claim: Ishihara et al. (2006) concluded that the findings did not support a gene dosage effect for LRRK2 G2019S.
checks.evidence_quote: the similarities between patients with homozygous and heterozygous mutations do not support a gene dosage effect.
checks.explanation: The conclusions state this directly.

paragraphs.text: Gehrke et al. (2010) found that pathogenic LRRK2 interferes with microRNA (miRNA)-mediated translational repression in Drosophila. Pathogenic Drosophila Lrrk (I1915T) and human LRRK2 (G2019S) antagonized the miRNAs let-7 and miR-184*, which repress translation of the dp and e2f1 mRNAs, respectively, and this led to overproduction of E2F1/DP. In HEK293T cells, LRRK2 G2019S and I2020T relieved let-7 repression of a reporter, and this effect depended on kinase activity. LRRK2 with the R1441G mutation had no such effect. LRRK2 associated with Drosophila Argonaute-1 and human Argonaute-2, and in aged fly brain pathogenic LRRK2 reduced Argonaute-1 protein levels. Pathogenic LRRK2 also promoted association of phosphorylated 4E-BP1 with human Argonaute-2. Removing 1 copy of e2f1 or dp suppressed the loss of dopaminergic neurons caused by pathogenic Lrrk, and increasing let-7 or miR-184* levels attenuated the effects of pathogenic LRRK2. Conversely, blocking let-7 or miR-184* function, or protecting dp mRNA from let-7, reproduced the dopaminergic neuron loss.

checks.claim: Gehrke et al. (2010) found that pathogenic LRRK2 interferes with microRNA-mediated translational repression in Drosophila.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we show that LRRK2 interacts with the microRNA (miRNA) pathway to regulate protein synthesis.
checks.explanation: The paper's central finding, demonstrated in Drosophila, is that pathogenic LRRK2 antagonizes miRNA-mediated translational repression.

checks.claim: Pathogenic Drosophila Lrrk (I1915T) and human LRRK2 (G2019S) antagonized the miRNAs let-7 and miR-184*.
checks.evidence_quote: Da-Gal4-directed ubiquitous or TH-Gal4-directed DN-specific co-expression of pathogenic dLRRK(I1915T) or hLRRK2(G2019S) all stimulated reporter expression, more so than WT proteins
checks.explanation: Both pathogenic forms antagonized the let-7 reporter, and pathogenic hLRRK2 relieved repression by both let-7 and miR-184*; the abstract states "Pathogenic LRRK2 antagonizes these miRNAs."

checks.claim: let-7 represses translation of dp mRNA and miR-184* represses translation of e2f1 mRNA.
checks.evidence_quote: One candidate miR-184*-binding site in e2f1-3′UTR responded to miR-184* activity in reporter assays (Fig.3a).
checks.explanation: The full text shows miR-184* targets e2f1 and let-7 targets dp ("one functional let-7-binding site within dp-3′UTR"; pre-let-7 reduced DP, pre-miR-184* reduced E2F1), matching the claim. The abstract's "respectively" wording is reversed relative to the full text.

checks.claim: Antagonism of let-7 and miR-184* by pathogenic LRRK2 led to overproduction of E2F1/DP.
checks.evidence_quote: Western blot analysis confirmed upregulation of E2F1 and DP by dLRRK(I1915T) or hLRRK2(G2019S) (Fig.2a, s12a,b)
checks.explanation: Pathogenic LRRK2 relieved miRNA repression of e2f1/dp 3'UTR reporters and raised E2F1 and DP protein without a change in mRNA level.

checks.claim: In HEK293T cells, LRRK2 G2019S and I2020T relieved let-7 repression of a reporter.
checks.evidence_quote: hLRRK2(I2020T) or hLRRK2(G2019S) efficiently suppressed the inhibitory effect of let-7 on reporter expression (Fig.s2a,s2b)
checks.explanation: Stated directly for HEK293T cells using a luciferase reporter with let-7-binding sites.

checks.claim: Relief of let-7 repression by LRRK2 G2019S and I2020T depended on kinase activity.
checks.evidence_quote: Introduction of kinase-inactivating mutations (3KD) into hLRRK2-G2019S or -I2020T abolished the effects of these proteins on reporter expression (Fig.s2b), supporting kinase activity-dependency of pathogenic LRRK2 action.
checks.explanation: Kinase-dead versions of both mutants lost the effect, establishing kinase dependence.

checks.claim: LRRK2 with the R1441G mutation did not relieve let-7 repression of a reporter.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutant hLRRK2 carrying another pathogenic mutation R1441G had no effect on let-7 miRNA function (Fig.s2b)
checks.explanation: Directly stated.

checks.claim: LRRK2 associated with Drosophila Argonaute-1 and human Argonaute-2.
checks.evidence_quote: transfected hLRRK2 associated with hAgo2 in HEK293T cells (Fig.1c), transgenic hLRRK2 associated with dAgo1 in fly head extracts (Fig.1f), and endogenous hLRRK2 or dLRRK associated with hAgo2 or dAgo1, respectively
checks.explanation: Co-IP demonstrated association with both Drosophila Ago1 and human Ago2.

checks.claim: In aged fly brain, pathogenic LRRK2 reduced Argonaute-1 protein levels.
checks.evidence_quote: in aged flies dAgo1 protein was significantly reduced by pathogenic hLRRK2 (Fig.1g, s5b)
checks.explanation: Directly stated; no significant change was seen in young flies.

checks.claim: Pathogenic LRRK2 promoted association of phosphorylated 4E-BP1 with human Argonaute-2.
checks.evidence_quote: Pathogenic hLRRK2 with hyperactive kinase activity thus promotes the association of phospho-4E-BP with hAgo2, relieving miRNA-mediated translational repression.
checks.explanation: Directly stated, based on 4E-BP1/hAgo2 co-IP experiments in HEK293T cells.

checks.claim: Removing 1 copy of e2f1 or dp suppressed the dopaminergic neuron loss caused by pathogenic Drosophila Lrrk.
checks.evidence_quote: removing one copy of e2f1 or dp, or overexpressing RBF, a negative regulator of E2F1/DP, suppressed the DN phenotypes in TH-Gal4>dLRRK(I1915T) animals (Fig.2c)
checks.explanation: Heterozygosity for e2f1 or dp suppressed the dopaminergic neuron phenotypes of pathogenic dLRRK.

checks.claim: Increasing let-7 or miR-184* levels attenuated the effects of pathogenic LRRK2.
checks.evidence_quote: DN-specific pre-let-7 or pre-miR-184* overexpression or mature miRNA injection partially rescued TH-Gal4>dLRRK(I1915T) mutant phenotypes
checks.explanation: Increasing either miRNA attenuated pathogenic LRRK2 phenotypes, as also stated in the abstract.

checks.claim: Blocking let-7 or miR-184* function reproduced dopaminergic neuron loss.
checks.evidence_quote: Anti-let-7fS and anti-miR-184*fS injection resulted in specific DN loss (Fig.4d, s15a, b), and reduced climbing activity (Fig.s9c).
checks.explanation: Antagomir blockage of either miRNA caused dopaminergic neuron loss; the let-7 deletion mutant also showed DN reduction.

checks.claim: Protecting dp mRNA from let-7 reproduced dopaminergic neuron loss.
checks.evidence_quote: TH-Gal4-driven dp-TPlet-7 expression led to DN loss and reduced climbing activity (Fig.4e, s9d, s19b)
checks.explanation: The dp target protector, which blocks the let-7/dp 3'UTR interaction, caused dopaminergic neuron loss.

paragraphs.text: Lee et al. (2010) identified compounds that inhibit LRRK2 kinase activity. Overexpression of LRRK2 G2019S caused neurite shortening and cell death in primary cortical neurons, whereas kinase-dead LRRK2 (D1994A) was not toxic. The inhibitors GW5074, indirubin-3-prime-monooxime, and sorafenib protected against G2019S toxicity, whereas compounds that did not inhibit LRRK2 kinase failed to protect. In mice, herpes simplex virus amplicon-mediated delivery of LRRK2 G2019S caused loss of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neurons in the substantia nigra; kinase-dead G2019S/D1994A did not. Twice-daily intraperitoneal GW5074 or indirubin-3-prime-monooxime attenuated this neuronal loss. Lee et al. (2010) concluded that LRRK2-induced neurodegeneration in vivo is kinase dependent.

checks.claim: Lee et al. (2010) identified compounds that inhibit LRRK2 kinase activity.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we identify inhibitors of LRRK2 kinase that are protective in in vitro and in vivo models of LRRK2-induced neurodegeneration.
checks.explanation: The paper's central finding is the identification of LRRK2 kinase inhibitors.

checks.claim: Overexpression of LRRK2 G2019S caused neurite shortening and cell death in primary cortical neurons.
checks.evidence_quote: Both LRRK2 WT and LRRK2 G2019S overexpression leads to primary cortical neuron injury as assessed by neurite shortening (Fig. 2a, b and Supplementary Fig. 3) and LRRK2 G2019S overexpression leads to cell death as assessed by DNA fragmentation
checks.explanation: Both neurite shortening and cell death in primary cortical neurons from G2019S overexpression are stated.

checks.claim: Kinase-dead LRRK2 (D1994A) was not toxic in primary cortical neurons.
checks.evidence_quote: whereas a kinase dead versions of LRRK2 WT (D1994A) and LRRK2 G2019S (G2019S, D1994) are devoid of toxicity as previously described
checks.explanation: The kinase-dead D1994A versions were devoid of toxicity in the cortical neuron assays.

checks.claim: The inhibitors GW5074, indirubin-3-prime-monooxime, and sorafenib protected against LRRK2 G2019S toxicity.
checks.evidence_quote: Treatment of the cortical cultures with 0.5 μM GW5074 and 0.5 μM indirubin-3′-monooxime, which inhibit both LRRK2 and LRRK1, attenuate LRRK2 G2019S cell injury and cell death (Fig. 2b, d). The Raf kinase inhibitor, Sorafenib (0.5 μM), which is relatively selective for LRRK2 (see Supplementary Table 3), also completely protects against LRRK2 G2019S toxicity
checks.explanation: All three named compounds protected against G2019S toxicity in vitro.

checks.claim: Compounds that did not inhibit LRRK2 kinase failed to protect against LRRK2 G2019S toxicity.
checks.evidence_quote: The Raf kinase inhibitor, ZM336372 (0.5 μM), which does not inhibit either LRRK2 or LRRK1 kinase activity fails to inhibit LRRK2 G2019S toxicity
checks.explanation: ZM336372 and indirubin, which do not inhibit LRRK2 kinase, failed to protect.

checks.claim: In mice, herpes simplex virus amplicon-mediated delivery of LRRK2 G2019S caused loss of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neurons in the substantia nigra.
checks.evidence_quote: HSV amplicon-mediated delivery of LRRK2 G2019S induces significant loss of TH-positive neurons 3 weeks after stereotaxic injection into the ipsilateral striatum of mice compared to LRRK2 WT and eGFP control viruses
checks.explanation: Loss of TH-positive nigral neurons after HSV amplicon delivery of G2019S is explicitly reported.

checks.claim: In mice, delivery of kinase-dead LRRK2 G2019S/D1994A did not cause loss of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neurons in the substantia nigra.
checks.evidence_quote: HSV amplicon-mediated delivery of LRRK2 G2019S, D1994A causes no neuronal loss similar to LRRK2 WT and GFP control viruses
checks.explanation: The kinase-dead double mutant caused no neuronal loss in vivo.

checks.claim: Twice-daily intraperitoneal GW5074 or indirubin-3-prime-monooxime attenuated LRRK2 G2019S-induced neuronal loss in mice.
checks.evidence_quote: Twice daily injections of the LRRK2 kinase inhibitors, GW5074 and indirubin-3′-monooxime, (2.5 mg/kg, i.p.) attenuate the loss of TH-positive neurons induced by HSV-LRRK2 G2019S/CMVeGFP compared to DMSO and indirubin injected controls
checks.explanation: Twice-daily i.p. dosing of both compounds attenuated the neuronal loss.

checks.claim: Lee et al. (2010) concluded that LRRK2-induced neurodegeneration in vivo is kinase dependent.
checks.evidence_quote: These results establish that LRRK2-induced degeneration of neurons in vivo is kinase dependent
checks.explanation: The abstract states this conclusion verbatim.

paragraphs.text: Nichols et al. (2005) suggested that screening for the G2019S mutation should be part of genetic testing for Parkinson disease, and Gilks et al. (2005) suggested that testing for this mutation would be important in management and genetic counseling. Orr-Urtreger et al. (2007) suggested that testing symptomatic patients may help establish the diagnosis. They considered the value of screening asymptomatic individuals questionable until the penetrance and age-dependent risk of the mutation are better defined. In a review, Dächsel and Farrer (2010) noted that predisposing mutations are diagnostically useful in early or atypical presentations.

paragraphs.text: Skipper et al. (2005) evaluated common variation across LRRK2 using tagging SNPs in a sporadic Parkinson disease case-control series of 932 individuals from the Chinese population. They identified a haplotype that markedly increased disease risk when present in 2 copies (OR = 5.5, 95% CI = 2.1-14.0, P = 0.0001).

paragraphs.text: Orr-Urtreger et al. (2007) studied Jewish Israeli patients with Parkinson disease. G2019S was the only LRRK2 mutation found, present in 14.8% of Ashkenazi patients and 2.7% of non-Ashkenazi patients. Among Ashkenazi patients, it was present in 26% of familial cases and 10.6% of apparently sporadic cases. Carrier frequencies in Ashkenazi and non-Ashkenazi controls were 2.4% and 0.4%, respectively. A common shared haplotype was found in nearly all carriers tested. Women and patients with a positive family history were significantly overrepresented among carriers, and age at onset was similar in carriers and noncarriers.

paragraphs.text: Choi et al. (2008) analyzed 72 unrelated Korean patients with early-onset Parkinson disease (onset at or before 50 years). Nine (12.5%) were heterozygous for the LRRK2 G2385R variant, previously identified as a susceptibility allele in Asian Parkinson disease, and none carried G2019S.

checks.evidence_quote: in 72 unrelated EOPD (age-at-onset <or=50) recruited from ten movement disorders clinics in South Korea
checks.explanation: The cohort size, the Korean origin and the onset cutoff of 50 years or younger all match the abstract.

checks.claim: Nine (12.5%) of 72 Korean early-onset Parkinson disease patients were heterozygous for the LRRK2 G2385R variant.
checks.evidence_quote: Nine patients (12.5%) had heterozygous G2385R polymorphism of LRRK2, whereas none had G2019S mutation.

checks.claim: None of 72 Korean early-onset Parkinson disease patients carried LRRK2 G2019S.
checks.evidence_quote: Nine patients (12.5%) had heterozygous G2385R polymorphism of LRRK2, whereas none had G2019S mutation.
checks.explanation: The abstract says no patient carried G2019S.

paragraphs.text: In a genomewide association study of 2,011 cases and 18,381 controls from Japan, Satake et al. (2009) found a strong association of Parkinson disease with LRRK2 on 12q12 (P = 2.72 x 10(-8)). Comparison with a study of individuals of European ancestry identified LRRK2 as a risk locus shared between the populations. Tan et al. (2010) studied 1,349 ethnic Chinese subjects and found that PARK8 SNPs were associated with an increased risk of Parkinson disease. A pooled analysis of the Chinese cohorts and 2 Japanese replication cohorts (1,366 cases and 16,669 controls) confirmed the association.

checks.claim: Satake et al. (2009) performed a genomewide association study of 2,011 Parkinson disease cases and 18,381 controls from Japan.
checks.evidence_quote: we performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) and two replication studies in a total of 2,011 cases and 18,381 controls from Japan.
checks.explanation: The case and control counts match. The paper's total also includes the two replication studies.

checks.claim: Satake et al. (2009) found a strong association of Parkinson disease with LRRK2 on 12q12 (P = 2.72 x 10(-8)).
checks.evidence_quote: We also detected strong associations at SNCA on 4q22 (P = 7.35 x 10(-17)) and LRRK2 on 12q12 (P = 2.72 x 10(-8))
checks.explanation: The locus and the P value match the abstract.

checks.claim: Comparison with a study of individuals of European ancestry identified LRRK2 as a Parkinson disease risk locus shared between Japanese and European populations.
checks.evidence_quote: By comparing results of a GWAS performed on individuals of European ancestry, we identified PARK16, SNCA and LRRK2 as shared risk loci for PD
checks.explanation: The abstract states that LRRK2 is a shared risk locus in the comparison with Europeans.

checks.claim: Tan et al. (2010) studied 1,349 ethnic Chinese subjects and found that PARK8 SNPs were associated with an increased risk of Parkinson disease.
checks.evidence_quote: PARK16 SNPs were associated with a decreased risk while PARK1 and PARK8 SNPs were associated with an increased risk of PD.
checks.explanation: The abstract reports 1,349 ethnic Chinese subjects and says PARK8 SNPs were linked to increased PD risk.

checks.claim: A pooled analysis of Chinese cohorts and 2 Japanese replication cohorts (1,366 cases and 16,669 controls) confirmed the association of PARK8 SNPs with Parkinson disease.
checks.evidence_quote: A pooled analysis of our Chinese cohorts and 2 Japanese replication cohorts involving 1,366 subjects with PD and 16,669 controls revealed robust association with these 3 loci and also BST1.
checks.explanation: The 3 loci are PARK16, PARK8 and PARK1, so the pooled analysis confirms the PARK8 association. The case and control counts match.

paragraphs.text: Alcalay et al. (2010) studied 953 patients with early-onset Parkinson disease (onset before 51 years) and found the LRRK2 G2019S mutation in 35 (3.6%). G2019S carriers were more likely than noncarriers to report Jewish ancestry.

checks.claim: Alcalay et al. (2010) studied 953 patients with early-onset Parkinson disease (onset before 51 years).
checks.evidence_quote: Nine hundred fifty-three individuals with early-onset PD defined as age at onset (AAO) younger than 51 years.
checks.explanation: The paper states the cohort size and the onset cutoff directly.

checks.claim: Alcalay et al. (2010) found LRRK2 G2019S in 35 (3.6%) of 953 early-onset Parkinson disease patients.
checks.evidence_quote: One hundred fifty-eight (16.6%) participants had mutations, including 64 (6.7%) PRKN, 35 (3.6%) LRRK2 G2019S, 64 (6.7%) GBA, and 1 (0.2%) DJ1.
checks.explanation: The abstract gives exactly 35 (3.6%). The Results section names 31 single-gene G2019S carriers, and Table 2 adds 4 more who also carry another mutation, for a total of 35.

checks.claim: LRRK2 G2019S carriers with early-onset Parkinson disease were more likely than noncarriers to report Jewish ancestry.
checks.evidence_quote: The association was driven by LRRK2 G2019S carriers and GBA N370S carriers who were more likely to be Jewish than non-Jewish (Table 4).
checks.explanation: Table 1 agrees: 55% of G2019S carriers reported Jewish ancestry, against 12% of non-carriers.

paragraphs.text: Liu et al. (2008) generated transgenic Drosophila expressing either wildtype human LRRK2 or LRRK2 G2019S. Expression of either form in photoreceptor cells caused retinal degeneration. Expression in neurons caused adult-onset selective loss of dopaminergic neurons, locomotor dysfunction, and early mortality, and G2019S produced a more severe phenotype than equivalent levels of wildtype LRRK2. Treatment with L-DOPA improved locomotor impairment but did not prevent loss of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neurons.

checks.claim: Liu et al. (2008) generated transgenic Drosophila expressing either wildtype human LRRK2 or LRRK2 G2019S.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we used the GAL4/UAS system to generate transgenic Drosophila expressing either wild-type human LRRK2 or LRRK2-G2019S, the most common mutation associated with PD.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: Expression of either wildtype human LRRK2 or LRRK2 G2019S in Drosophila photoreceptor cells caused retinal degeneration.
checks.evidence_quote: Expression of either wild-type human LRRK2 or LRRK2-G2019S in the photoreceptor cells caused retinal degeneration.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: Neuronal expression of human LRRK2 in Drosophila caused adult-onset selective loss of dopaminergic neurons.
checks.evidence_quote: Expression of LRRK2 or LRRK2-G2019S in neurons produced adult-onset selective loss of dopaminergic neurons, locomotor dysfunction, and early mortality.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: Neuronal expression of human LRRK2 in Drosophila caused locomotor dysfunction.
checks.evidence_quote: Expression of LRRK2 or LRRK2-G2019S in neurons produced adult-onset selective loss of dopaminergic neurons, locomotor dysfunction, and early mortality.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: Neuronal expression of human LRRK2 in Drosophila caused early mortality.
checks.evidence_quote: Expression of LRRK2 or LRRK2-G2019S in neurons produced adult-onset selective loss of dopaminergic neurons, locomotor dysfunction, and early mortality.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: LRRK2 G2019S produced a more severe phenotype in Drosophila than equivalent levels of wildtype LRRK2.
checks.evidence_quote: Expression of mutant G2019S-LRRK2 caused a more severe parkinsonism-like phenotype than expression of equivalent levels of wild-type LRRK2.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: L-DOPA treatment improved locomotor impairment in LRRK2 transgenic Drosophila.
checks.evidence_quote: Treatment with l-DOPA improved mutant LRRK2-induced locomotor impairment but did not prevent the loss of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neurons.
checks.explanation: The paper says the improvement was in locomotor impairment caused by mutant LRRK2. The claim refers more broadly to LRRK2 transgenic flies.

checks.claim: L-DOPA treatment did not prevent loss of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neurons in LRRK2 transgenic Drosophila.
checks.evidence_quote: Treatment with l-DOPA improved mutant LRRK2-induced locomotor impairment but did not prevent the loss of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neurons.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly. The context is the mutant LRRK2 flies.

paragraphs.text: Zimprich et al. (2004) identified disease-segregating LRRK2 mutations in families with autosomal dominant parkinsonism, including family D from western Nebraska, originally described by Wszolek et al. (1995). Nandhagopal et al. (2008) reported that family D carries the arg1441-to-cys (R1441C) mutation. PET imaging of presymptomatic mutation carriers in this family showed dopaminergic dysfunction that progressed over time.

checks.claim: Zimprich et al. (2004) identified disease-segregating LRRK2 mutations in families with autosomal dominant parkinsonism, including family D.
checks.evidence_quote: Within affected carriers of families A and D, six post mortem diagnoses reveal brainstem dopaminergic degeneration
checks.explanation: The abstract refers to affected mutation carriers in family D, so family D is among the families with LRRK2 mutations. The western Nebraska origin is not in this abstract, but it is attributed to another source in the draft.

checks.claim: Family D is from western Nebraska and was originally described by Wszolek et al. (1995).
checks.evidence_quote: Western Nebraska family (family D) with autosomal dominant parkinsonism.
checks.explanation: The title identifies family D as a western Nebraska family described in this 1995 paper.

checks.claim: Nandhagopal et al. (2008) reported that family D carries the LRRK2 arg1441-to-cys (R1441C) mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: parkinsonian kindred (family D, Western Nebraska) carrying LRRK2 (R1441C) mutation.
checks.explanation: The abstract reports that family D carries R1441C; arg1441-to-cys is the same variant in different notation.

checks.claim: PET imaging of presymptomatic LRRK2 R1441C mutation carriers in family D showed dopaminergic dysfunction.
checks.evidence_quote: PET study of presymptomatic members of our LRRK2 kindred revealed dopaminergic dysfunction that progressed over time.
checks.explanation: The abstract says PET of presymptomatic kindred members, who are described as R1441C carriers, showed dopaminergic dysfunction.

checks.claim: Dopaminergic dysfunction in presymptomatic LRRK2 R1441C carriers in family D progressed over time.
checks.evidence_quote: PET study of presymptomatic members of our LRRK2 kindred revealed dopaminergic dysfunction that progressed over time.
checks.explanation: The abstract says the dysfunction progressed over time.

paragraphs.text: Nichols et al. (2005) found the gly2019-to-ser (G2019S) mutation in 35 (5%) of 767 affected individuals from 358 multiplex families with Parkinson disease. Thirty-four were heterozygous and 1 was homozygous, and all had typical clinical findings of idiopathic Parkinson disease.

checks.claim: Nichols et al. (2005) found the LRRK2 gly2019-to-ser (G2019S) mutation in 35 (5%) of 767 affected individuals from 358 multiplex families with Parkinson disease.
checks.evidence_quote: Of 767 affected individuals from 358 multiplex families, 35 (5%) individuals were either heterozygous (34) or homozygous (one) for the mutation
checks.explanation: Matches; the mutation is Gly2019Ser.

checks.claim: Of 35 LRRK2 G2019S carriers found by Nichols et al. (2005), 34 were heterozygous and 1 was homozygous.
checks.evidence_quote: 35 (5%) individuals were either heterozygous (34) or homozygous (one) for the mutation
checks.explanation: Matches.

checks.claim: All LRRK2 G2019S carriers found by Nichols et al. (2005) had typical clinical findings of idiopathic Parkinson disease.
checks.evidence_quote: and had typical clinical findings of idiopathic Parkinson's disease.
checks.explanation: Matches.

paragraphs.text: Di Fonzo et al. (2005) found the heterozygous G2019S mutation in 4 of 61 (6.6%) unrelated families with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease from Italy, Portugal, and Brazil.

checks.claim: Di Fonzo et al. (2005) found the heterozygous LRRK2 G2019S mutation in 4 of 61 (6.6%) unrelated families with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease.
checks.evidence_quote: identified a heterozygous mutation (Gly2019 ser) present in four of 61 (6.6%) unrelated families with Parkinson's disease and autosomal dominant inheritance
checks.explanation: The variant, zygosity and counts all match the abstract.

checks.claim: The autosomal dominant Parkinson disease families studied by Di Fonzo et al. (2005) were from Italy, Portugal, and Brazil.
checks.evidence_quote: The families originated from Italy, Portugal, and Brazil, indicating the presence of the mutation in different populations.
checks.explanation: In the abstract, these origins refer to the 4 families carrying the mutation. The origins of all 61 families studied aren't given, and the claim's wording could be read as covering all of them.

paragraphs.text: Gilks et al. (2005) found the heterozygous G2019S mutation, caused by a 2877510G-A change, in 8 (1.6%) of 482 patients with idiopathic Parkinson disease.

checks.claim: The LRRK2 G2019S mutation is caused by a 2877510G-A change.
checks.evidence_quote: a common heterozygous mutation, 2877510 g-->A, which produces a glycine to serine aminoacid substitution at codon 2019 (Gly2019 ser)
checks.explanation: The abstract names 2877510G-A as the nucleotide change that produces Gly2019Ser.

checks.claim: Gilks et al. (2005) found the heterozygous LRRK2 G2019S mutation in 8 (1.6%) of 482 patients with idiopathic Parkinson disease.
checks.evidence_quote: We assessed 482 patients with the disorder, of whom 263 had pathologically confirmed disease, by direct sequencing for mutations in exon 41 of LRRK2. The mutation was present in eight (1.6%) patients.
checks.explanation: The abstract gives 8 (1.6%) of 482 patients with idiopathic Parkinson disease, and it calls the mutation heterozygous.

paragraphs.text: Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2005) found the heterozygous G2019S mutation in 2 of 23 probands with dominantly inherited Parkinson disease and showed that it segregated completely with the disease in a large family.

checks.claim: Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2005) found the heterozygous LRRK2 G2019S mutation in 2 of 23 probands with dominantly inherited Parkinson disease.
checks.evidence_quote: The authors identified three probands with heterozygous LRRK2 mutations: two of them have the known G2019S substitution
checks.explanation: Two of the 23 probands from dominant PD families carried heterozygous G2019S.

checks.claim: Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2005) showed that LRRK2 G2019S segregated completely with Parkinson disease in a large family.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutation analysis of a large family demonstrated complete segregation of the G2019S with PD.
checks.explanation: The paper states complete segregation in a large family.

paragraphs.text: Ishihara et al. (2006) described 29 Parkinson disease patients homozygous for the 6055G-A (G2019S) mutation, from Tunisia, Algeria, the US, Canada, and Morocco. Their phenotype was indistinguishable from that of heterozygous patients.

checks.evidence_quote: To report the clinical characteristics of PD patients with homozygous LRRK2 6055G>A (G2019S) mutations
checks.explanation: The abstract gives the mutation as 6055G>A (G2019S). Its per-country counts (23+2+2+1+1) add up to 29 patients.

checks.claim: The 29 Parkinson disease patients homozygous for LRRK2 G2019S described by Ishihara et al. (2006) came from Tunisia, Algeria, the US, Canada, and Morocco.
checks.evidence_quote: Patients with familial PD and homozygous LRRK2 mutations included 23 Tunisians, 2 Algerians, 2 US patients, 1 Canadian, and 1 Moroccan.
checks.explanation: The countries of origin listed match the claim.

checks.claim: The phenotype of Parkinson disease patients homozygous for LRRK2 G2019S could not be told apart from that of heterozygous G2019S patients.
checks.evidence_quote: There were no observable differences between the homozygote and heterozygote phenotypes.
checks.explanation: The abstract's finding of no observable differences supports describing the homozygous phenotype as indistinguishable from the heterozygous one.

paragraphs.text: Lesage et al. (2005) reported a common founder for the G2019S mutation dating from the 13th century in European and North African families. Lesage et al. (2009) found G2019S in 13 (5.8%) of 226 probands from families with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease, including 6 from North Africa (43%).

checks.explanation: The title links the common founder to the European and North African families.

checks.claim: Lesage et al. (2005) dated the common founder of the LRRK2 G2019S mutation to the 13th century.
checks.evidence_quote: a common founder for the G2019S mutation dating from the 13th century
checks.explanation: The title states the 13th-century dating.

checks.claim: Lesage et al. (2009) found the LRRK2 G2019S mutation in 13 (5.8%) of 226 probands from families with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease.

checks.evidence_quote: The common p.G2019S mutation was identified in 13 probands (5.8%) including six from North Africa (43%).
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

paragraphs.text: Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2005) identified a novel heterozygous ile1371-to-val (I1371V) substitution in LRRK2 in 1 of 23 probands from families with dominantly inherited Parkinson disease. (2009) found the heterozygous I1371V mutation in 2 probands from families with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease.

checks.claim: Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2005) identified a novel heterozygous ile1371-to-val (I1371V) substitution in LRRK2 in 1 of 23 probands from families with dominantly inherited Parkinson disease.

checks.claim: Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2005) evaluated LRRK2 mutation frequencies in 180 neurologically normal controls.

checks.claim: Lesage et al. (2009) found the heterozygous LRRK2 I1371V mutation in 2 probands from families with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease.
checks.evidence_quote: The known heterozygous p.R1441H and p.I1371V mutations were found in two probands each
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Lesage et al. (2009) found the known heterozygous LRRK2 arg1441-to-his (R1441H) mutation in 2 probands from a series of 226 families with Parkinson disease compatible with autosomal dominant inheritance.
